question.problem: Find the set of values of $z$ that satisfy $1-z>3$ and $2z+1>5.$
question.worked_solution:
To solve the system, we solve each inequality separately and then find their intersection.

- First, we solve $1-z>3:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}1-z & >3 \\ 1-z-1 & >3-1 \\ -z & >2 \\ (-1)\cdot (-z) & <(-1)\cdot 2 \\ z & <-2\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14194110/assets/72d4febdc48282faebade8f8a4b827a72b82433b054c6409752f892cb718ec85.png)

- Then, we solve $2z+1>5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2z+1 & >5 \\ 2z+1-1 & >5-1 \\ 2z & >4 \\ \frac{2z}{2} & >\frac{4}{2} \\ z & >2\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14194110/assets/84893a305567a0aaaafb6fd2393c62f05086780ce8c8a55b91ba68676ba309ce.png)

To find the values of $z$ that satisfy both inequalities, we find where the two solutions overlap:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14194110/assets/04b20be3eaf236e70aa5bdf8cf6e25b6838b3bb823fe16f926112fb1f5e02d6f.png)

It turns out that the solutions do not overlap at all. Therefore, there are no values of $z$ that satisfy both inequalities simultaneously. So, there is no solution.
